reason: The sources provide 12 multi-sourced claims supporting a compelling 45-second story about the starburst dwarf galaxy NGC 4449.
story: In 1788, astronomer William Herschel discovered NGC 4449, a dwarf irregular galaxy located in the constellation Canes Venatici. Also known as Caldwell 21, this object is part of a galaxy group in the northern sky. Although it is a small dwarf system, NGC 4449 is far from quiet. It is classified as a starburst galaxy undergoing an exceptionally high rate of star formation. Gravitational interactions with neighboring galaxies are believed to have triggered this cosmic fury, igniting massive waves of new stars throughout the system. Telescope images of NGC 4449 reveal vibrant bluish-white regions packed with young, massive stars alongside glowing pinkish clouds of gas where brand new stars are actively flaring into life.
angle: Gravitational interactions with neighboring galaxies have ignited an intense starburst across dwarf galaxy NGC 4449, lighting it up with brilliant pink star nurseries and blue star clusters.

disputed: Distance to Earth: S1 states NGC 4449 is located about 13 million light-years away, whereas S2 states 10 million light-years. Script handling: leave out specific distance numbers due to disagreement.

Starburst extending to galaxy edge and early universe comparison: S2 mentions starburst activity reaching the galaxy edge and serving as a model for early universe galaxies, but S1 does not mention these points. Script handling: leave out as single-sourced.

Interaction details with specific dwarf satellites: S1 details the 2012 discovery of two tidally disrupted satellite galaxies being absorbed, which S2 does not mention. Script handling: leave out as single-sourced.
